newsitem.title: THAILAND: U.S. rights group accuses Burma of holding students.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rights group accuses Burma of holding students.

text.p: U.S.-based human rights group Human Rights Watch/Asia said on Tuesday that scores of Burmese students detained after recent street protests were still being held incommunicado by the military government.
It added that 10 members of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) were also being held since the weekend by the authorities.
There has been no NLD comment on the alleged arrests.

"We are concerned about the safety of those in detention and by reports that at least two demonstrators may have been seriously injured on Friday night," the rights group said in a statement received here.
The military has said it detained some 860 students in protests over the past week but released all of them shortly afterwards.

Human Rights Watch/Asia also said at least three freelance journalists visiting Burma on tourist visas from Norway, France and Netherlands had been deported, and accused the government of blocking independent coverage of the Burmese student unrest.
The group urged Burma to "immediately end all acts of violence and intimidation gainst journalists."
A spokesman for Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) said on Monday a Dutch journalist had been deported for failing to have the correct visa.
Human Rights Watch/Asia called on the SLORC to let the U.N. Special Rapporteur to Burma, Rajsoomer Lallah, visit the country to investigate the unrest and detentions.
Lallah was said to be currently visiting Thailand, but U.N. sources in Bangkok said he was not in the country.
Students from Rangoon universities have launched several anti-government street protests in the past week. The military broke up the demonstrations and briefly detained more than 860 people.
Over the weekend, students at two northern Mandalay universities also staged protest rallies, diplomats said.
The latest protests were the biggest seen in the capital since the student-led pro-democracy uprisings of September 1988, which the military crushed, leaving thousands dead or in jail.
The students have demanded more freedom and rights, and protested against police brutality in handling a brawl between some students and restaurant owners in October.
A government spokesman on Monday blamed some NLD members, student exiles and communist elements for instigating the latest unrest. The military was flushing out these elements, he added.
Suu Kyi has denied that the NLD was linked to the protests.

Troops and police sealed off access to Yangon University and the Yangon Institute of Technology. Most classes were cancelled as hundreds of boarding students left for home fearing campuses may be closed.
